subChunks.title: Component Architecture at Scale
subChunks.hookHtml: Small component libraries are designed bottom-up: you build the components you need. Large-scale component systems are designed top-down: you define rules, then build components that follow them. Headless components separate logic from presentation so you can swap styling systems. Compound components create APIs that feel native. Controlled vs uncontrolled patterns determine who owns state. These are the architectural decisions that determine whether a component library scales to 100 components or collapses under its own weight.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Headless component pattern

// Headless: logic without rendering — consumer provides UI
// This is how Radix UI, Headless UI, and TanStack Table work:

export function useSelect<T>(items: T[], getKey: (item: T) => string) {
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState<T | null>(null);
  const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false);
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');

  const filtered = items.filter(item =>
    getKey(item).toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase())
  );

  return {
    selected,
    isOpen,
    query,
    filtered,
    select: setSelected,
    toggle: () => setIsOpen(o => !o),
    search: setQuery,
    getItemProps: (item: T) => ({  // Spreads onto item elements
      onClick: () => { setSelected(item); setIsOpen(false); },
      'aria-selected': selected === item,
      role: 'option' as const,
    }),
    getTriggerProps: () => ({  // Spreads onto trigger button
      onClick: () => setIsOpen(o => !o),
      'aria-expanded': isOpen,
      'aria-haspopup': 'listbox' as const,
    }),
  };
}

// Consumer controls the UI:
function GuildSelect({ guilds }: { guilds: Guild[] }) {
  const select = useSelect(guilds, g => g.name);
  return (
    <div>
      <button {...select.getTriggerProps()}>{select.selected?.name ?? 'Select guild'}</button>
      {select.isOpen && (
        <ul role="listbox">
          {select.filtered.map(guild => (
            <li key={guild.id} {...select.getItemProps(guild)}>{guild.name}</li>
          ))}
        </ul>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

Compound component with Context

// Compound components: related components that share implicit state
// Like HTML's <select> + <option> — they work together

type TabsContextValue = { activeTab: string; setActiveTab: (id: string) => void };
const TabsContext = createContext<TabsContextValue | null>(null);

function useTabs() {
  const ctx = useContext(TabsContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('Tab components must be used inside <Tabs>');
  return ctx;
}

export function Tabs({ children, defaultTab }: { children: ReactNode; defaultTab: string }) {
  const [activeTab, setActiveTab] = useState(defaultTab);
  return (
    <TabsContext.Provider value={{ activeTab, setActiveTab }}>
      {children}
    </TabsContext.Provider>
  );
}

Tabs.List = function TabList({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return <div role="tablist">{children}</div>;
};

Tabs.Tab = function Tab({ id, children }: { id: string; children: ReactNode }) {
  const { activeTab, setActiveTab } = useTabs();
  return (
    <button
      role="tab"
      aria-selected={activeTab === id}
      onClick={() => setActiveTab(id)}
    >
      {children}
    </button>
  );
};

Tabs.Panel = function TabPanel({ id, children }: { id: string; children: ReactNode }) {
  const { activeTab } = useTabs();
  return activeTab === id ? <div role="tabpanel">{children}</div> : null;
};

// Usage — reads like prose:
<Tabs defaultTab="quests">
  <Tabs.List>
    <Tabs.Tab id="quests">Quests</Tabs.Tab>
    <Tabs.Tab id="members">Members</Tabs.Tab>
  </Tabs.List>
  <Tabs.Panel id="quests"><QuestBoard /></Tabs.Panel>
  <Tabs.Panel id="members"><MemberList /></Tabs.Panel>
</Tabs>

Controlled vs uncontrolled

// Support both patterns — parent can opt in to control:
interface SelectProps {
  // Uncontrolled — component owns state:
  defaultValue?: string;
  // Controlled — parent owns state:
  value?: string;
  onChange?: (value: string) => void;
}

function Select({ defaultValue, value: controlledValue, onChange }: SelectProps) {
  const isControlled = controlledValue !== undefined;
  const [internalValue, setInternalValue] = useState(defaultValue ?? '');
  const value = isControlled ? controlledValue : internalValue;

  function handleChange(newValue: string) {
    if (!isControlled) setInternalValue(newValue);
    onChange?.(newValue);
  }

  return <select value={value} onChange={e => handleChange(e.target.value)}>...</select>;
}

Vex: "The headless pattern is the most important shift in component architecture of the last five years. It separates the hard problem (managing complex state and accessibility behaviour) from the easy problem (styling). Radix UI solved the hard problems once; your design system skins it. You never rebuild focus trapping or keyboard navigation again."

storyBeats.text: The design team wants the Select component to look completely different. The logic — filtering, keyboard navigation, accessibility — stays the same. With a headless component, the UI is swapped in minutes. Without it: a complete rewrite.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Headless is not about abstractions for the sake of abstractions. It's about separating the two problems that change at different rates: interaction logic (rarely) and visual design (frequently). A compound component's API is a DSL — it should read like the domain it models. Tabs.Tab, Tabs.Panel, Tabs.List. Not Tab, TabContent, TabList.

storyBeats.speaker: Compound component API — reads like intent

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a compound Tabs component:

  • Create Tabs, Tabs.List, Tabs.Tab, and Tabs.Panel using context to share active tab state
  • Add proper ARIA attributes: role=tablist on List, role=tab + aria-selected on Tab, role=tabpanel on Panel
  • Support both controlled (value + onChange) and uncontrolled (defaultTab) usage
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a production-grade component architecture: (1) A headless useCombobox hook that manages filtering, selection, keyboard navigation (arrow keys, Enter, Escape), and generates prop getters for the trigger, input, listbox, and each option. (2) A Combobox component that uses useCombobox with your design system's visual layer. (3) A compound Accordion component (Accordion, Accordion.Item, Accordion.Trigger, Accordion.Content) with single/multi-open modes via a controlled/uncontrolled API. (4) Storybook stories for both components documenting all variants and states. Verify keyboard accessibility with a screen reader.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the headless component pattern — what does it separate, and why does that separation matter for design system maintainability? Walk through compound components: how does the context-sharing pattern work, and why throw an error if useTabs() is called outside Tabs? Explain controlled vs uncontrolled components — what is the rule about not mixing them (switching from uncontrolled to controlled), and how does a dual-mode component handle both?

questions.prompt: A Select component is uncontrolled (manages its own state). A parent component needs to reset the Select when a form is submitted. What is the cleanest approach?
options: Change the component's key prop — React unmounts and remounts a component when its key changes, resetting all internal state to the default. This is the React-sanctioned way to reset uncontrolled component state.
Add a reset() method to the component using useImperativeHandle
Convert the component to controlled and pass value/onChange from the parent
Use a ref to directly modify the component's state
questions.answer: Change the component's key prop — React unmounts and remounts a component when its key changes, resetting all internal state to the default. This is the React-sanctioned way to reset uncontrolled component state.
questions.explanation: key prop changes force React to treat a component as a completely new instance, unmounting the old one and mounting a fresh one with default state. This is explicitly documented by the React team as the correct pattern for resetting uncontrolled component state. It's cleaner than adding a reset() imperative API, and avoids making an uncontrolled component controlled (which React warns about as a controlled/uncontrolled switch).

questions.prompt: Your design system has a Dropdown component built from scratch with custom positioning logic. Radix UI's DropdownMenu component is available. When should you use Radix vs your custom component?
options: Radix for new work — it provides battle-tested accessibility, keyboard navigation, portal-based positioning, and focus management for free. Custom components rarely implement all these correctly. Reserve custom only when Radix doesn't fit the interaction model.
Always use the custom component — external dependencies add bundle weight
Radix for simple dropdowns, custom for complex ones with business logic
Custom component only — design systems should be self-contained with no external UI dependencies
questions.answer: Radix for new work — it provides battle-tested accessibility, keyboard navigation, portal-based positioning, and focus management for free. Custom components rarely implement all these correctly. Reserve custom only when Radix doesn't fit the interaction model.
questions.explanation: Accessible dropdown implementation requires: focus trapping, keyboard navigation (arrow keys, Home, End, character search), portal positioning to escape overflow:hidden containers, proper ARIA attributes (menu, menuitem, aria-expanded), outside click dismissal, and escape key handling. Custom implementations routinely miss several of these. Radix (and similar headless libraries) solve these once. Your design system skins them. The cost: an external dependency with its own API surface and update cycle.
